Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
value.conclusion: dim_H(F)=dim_H(E)+1, equivalently dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1, in the stipulated Euclidean metric, including n=0.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of an extended metric space
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space X and A⊆X, diam(A)=sup{edist(x,y):x,y∈A}, with diam(∅)=0. On an ordinary metric space edist is the usual distance embedded in [0,∞], and unbounded sets have diameter ∞. On a bounded set in an ordinary metric space the diameter is a nonnegative real. For every nonnegative integer m, Euclidean space ℝ^m has distance (sum_{j=1}^m (x_j-y_j)^2)^(1/2); ℝ^0 is a singleton. All Euclidean sets below use this metric.

definitions.type: scale contents H^s_δ and unnormalized Hausdorff measures H^s, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension.

definitions.type: native unnormalized Hausdorff measure family on extended metric spaces
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space X equipped with its Borel measurable structure, h^a(A) denotes Mathlib's MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a evaluated on A⊆X. For every real exponent a this is the metric outer-measure construction from the gauge r↦r^a on [0,∞], with empty covering sets contributing zero. At exponent zero the native convention is used; at every positive exponent 0^a=0. Values on arbitrary sets mean outer measure, so no measurability of A is stipulated.

binders.type: extended metric space with Borel measurable structure

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of a set in an extended metric space, in [0,∞]
definitions.definition: dim_H(A) is the usual Hausdorff dimension, represented by native dimH: sup{a∈[0,∞): h^a(A)=∞}, where the supremum is in [0,∞] and sup∅=0. The nonnegative finite exponents are regarded as elements of [0,∞]. This definition in particular uses the convention dim_H(∅)=0. When the dimension is finite it is identified with its nonnegative real value.

binders.type: extended metric space with its Borel structure

definitions.definition: I=[0,1], the closed unit interval with Euclidean distance.
F=E×I. The identification (x,t)↦(x_1,…,x_n,t) of ℝ^n×ℝ with ℝ^(n+1) is fixed throughout; dist((x,t),(y,u))=(dist(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2)^(1/2). No maximum product norm is used.
D=dim_H(E). Once finiteness is proved, D is also used for its corresponding nonnegative real value.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on ℝ and nonnegative integral notation
definitions.definition: λ is Lebesgue measure on ℝ with its Borel measurable structure (or its completion). For a measurable set B, |B|=λ(B). Integrals of nonnegative functions and series take values in [0,∞]; ∫_I means integration against the restriction λ|I. For a set J, 1_J is its indicator, taking values 0 and 1. A countable sum of nonnegative terms is the supremum of its finite partial sums.

1: # Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
6: Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
7: Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
8: Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).
9: 
10: > 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
11: > \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
12: > \(\mathbb R\).
13: 
14: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
15: 
16: Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
17: 2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
18: \(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
19: the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.
20: 
21: Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
22: compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
23: with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove
24: 
25: \[
26: \dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
27: \]
28: 
29: The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
30: formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
31: 
32: ## Fixed natural-language proof
33: 
34: For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put
35: 
36: \[
37: H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
38:  A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
39: \qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
40: \]
41: 
42: Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
43: unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
44: its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
45: \(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
46: Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
47: measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).
48: 
49: Write \(D=\dim_H E\) and \(F=E\times[0,1]\). First \(0\leq D\leq n\).
50: Indeed, compactness makes \(E\) bounded. When \(n>0\), a box containing
51: it admits a cover by at most \(Ch^{-n}\) cubes of side at most \(h\),
52: for \(0<h\leq1\). Here \(C\) depends only on that box. Each cube has
53: diameter at most \(\sqrt n h\). For any \(s>n\), the total \(s\)-cost
54: is at most \(C n^{s/2}h^{s-n}\to0\). These arbitrarily fine covers
55: give \(H^s(E)=0\) and hence \(D\leq n\). If \(n=0\), nonemptiness
56: makes \(E=\mathbb R^0\), a singleton of zero \(s\)-cost for every
57: \(s>0\); thus \(D=0\).
58: 
59: ### Upper bound
60: 
61: When \(n=0\), \(F\) is isometric to \([0,1]\). Dividing this interval
62: into \(N\) equal pieces gives total \(a\)-cost \(N^{1-a}\to0\) for
63: every \(a>1\), proving \(\dim_H F\leq1=D+1\).
64: For this upper-bound argument now assume \(n\geq1\).
65: 
66: Fix \(q>D\). Since \(q>0\) and \(H^q(E)=0\), for every
67: \(0<r\leq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a countable cover
68: \((U_i)\) of \(E\) with nonempty-member diameters
69: \(0<r_i\leq r\) and \(\sum_i r_i^q<\varepsilon\).
70: The positive-diameter requirement costs nothing: start with a cover of
71: cost below \(\varepsilon/2\); replace each zero-diameter singleton by
72: a ball of diameter at most \(r\), choosing the \(i\)-th replacement
73: to have \(q\)-cost less than \(\varepsilon2^{-i-2}\). The added cost
74: is less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Discard empty members.
75: 
76: Let \(N_i=\lceil1/r_i\rceil\). Partition \([0,1]\) into \(N_i\)
77: closed intervals of length \(1/N_i\leq r_i\). Because \(r_i\leq1\),
78: \(N_i\leq2/r_i\). The corresponding products with \(U_i\) form a
79: countable cover of \(F\). Each has Euclidean diameter at most
80: \(\sqrt2 r_i\), and their total \((q+1)\)-cost is at most
81: 
82: \[
83: \sum_iN_i(\sqrt2 r_i)^{q+1}
84: \leq2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\sum_i r_i^q
85: <2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\varepsilon.
86: \]
87: 
88: For any target scale \(\delta>0\), choose
89: \(r\leq\min(1,\delta/\sqrt2)\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
90: Thus \(H^{q+1}_\delta(F)=0\) for every scale, so
91: \(H^{q+1}(F)=0\) and \(\dim_H F\leq q+1\). Letting \(q\downarrow D\)
92: gives \(\dim_H F\leq D+1\).
93: 
94: ### Lower bound when \(D>0\)
95: 
96: Fix \(0<s<D\). Then \(H^s(E)=\infty\), so
97: \(H^s_\delta(E)\) becomes arbitrarily large as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
98: We claim that, for every \(\delta>0\),
99: 
100: \[
101: H^s_\delta(E)\leq H^{s+1}_\delta(F).                 \tag{1}
102: \]
103: 
104: Take an arbitrary countable \(\delta\)-cover \((V_i)_{i\geq0}\) of
105: \(F\), discarding empty members. Define
106: \(\rho_i=\operatorname{diam}V_i\),
107: \(A_i=\pi_{\mathbb R^n}(V_i)\), and
108: \(B_i=\pi_{\mathbb R}(V_i)\). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz,
109: so both projected diameters are at most \(\rho_i\leq\delta\).
110: For \(\varepsilon>0\), put
111: 
112: \[
113: \eta_i=\frac{\varepsilon2^{-i-1}}{1+\rho_i^s}>0.
114: \]
115: 
116: Enclose \(B_i\) in an open interval \(J_i\) of length at most
117: \(\rho_i+\eta_i\): its supremum minus infimum is at most \(\rho_i\),
118: and an enlargement of total width \(\eta_i\) suffices. This avoids
119: assuming that the arbitrary covering sets or their projections are measurable.
120: 
121: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), the sets \(A_i\) for which \(t\in J_i\)
122: cover \(E\). Indeed, a point \((x,t)\in F\) belongs to some \(V_i\),
123: giving \(x\in A_i\) and \(t\in B_i\subset J_i\). Their diameters
124: are at most \(\rho_i\). Consequently, with \(c=H^s_\delta(E)\),
125: 
126: \[
127: c\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s\mathbf1_{J_i}(t)\quad(t\in[0,1]).
128: \]
129: 
130: The constant \(c\) is finite: compactness gives a finite cover of \(E\)
131: by balls of diameter at most \(\delta\), with finite \(s\)-cost.
132: Each summand is nonnegative and measurable since \(J_i\) is open.
133: Integrate over \([0,1]\), of Lebesgue measure one, and use Tonelli's
134: theorem for this nonnegative series. Since
135: \(|J_i\cap[0,1]|\leq\rho_i+\eta_i\),
136: 
137: \[
138: \begin{aligned}
139: c&\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s|J_i\cap[0,1]|\\
140:  &\leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\sum_i\eta_i\rho_i^s
141:  \leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\varepsilon.
142: \end{aligned}
143: \]
144: 
145: If the first series is infinite the desired inequality is immediate;
146: otherwise let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Take the infimum over the
147: arbitrary covers to obtain (1). As its left side is unbounded at small
148: scales, \(H^{s+1}(F)=\infty\), giving \(\dim_H F\geq s+1\).
149: Letting \(s\uparrow D\) proves \(\dim_H F\geq D+1\).
150: 
151: ### Lower bound when \(D=0\)
152: 
153: Choose \(x_0\in E\). The map \(t\mapsto(x_0,t)\) is an isometric
154: embedding of \([0,1]\) into \(F\), so dimension monotonicity gives
155: \(\dim_H F\geq\dim_H[0,1]\). This interval has dimension one:
156: equal-length covers gave the upper bound above. For \(0<s<1\), any
157: \(\delta\)-cover with diameters \(\rho_i\leq\delta\) satisfies
158: \(\sum_i\rho_i\geq1\). To see this, enclose its nonempty members
159: in open intervals of lengths at most \(\rho_i+\varepsilon2^{-i-1}\),
160: use countable subadditivity of length to get
161: \(1\leq\sum_i\rho_i+\varepsilon\), and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
162: Hence \(\sum_i\rho_i^s\geq\delta^{s-1}\sum_i\rho_i
163: \geq\delta^{s-1}\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
164: This proves the lower bound one. Thus \(\dim_H F\geq1=D+1\),
165: including when \(n=0\).
166: 
167: Together the bounds establish the required equality.
168:

source_steps.text: Fix m≥0 and A⊆ℝ^m, and fix a real s. Temporarily assume L1: s>0. Apply M001 to X=ℝ^m with its Euclidean extended metric and Borel structure, a=s, and set A. For any finite positive scale δ0 its inner infimum is exactly the supplied H^s_δ0(A): nonempty bounded members have the same real and extended diameters, their powers agree, and empty members contribute zero in both conventions. A countable cover can be padded by empty members to be indexed by ℕ; conversely a sequence is countable. The supremum over positive extended scales equals the supremum over positive finite real scales. Indeed both content families increase when the scale decreases, and any fixed finite scale gives at least the content at scale ∞. Thus the term at ∞ cannot increase the supremum. Consequently F001: H^s(A)=h^s(A). No covering-set measurability was used.

The dimension is nonnegative by its supremum definition D004. Still under L1, apply M002, M003, M004 and M005 respectively with X=ℝ^m, its Borel structure, the current set A, and nonnegative exponent s. Under L2: s<dim_H(A), M002 and F001 give H^s(A)=∞; discharge L2. Under L3: dim_H(A)<s, M003 and F001 give H^s(A)=0; discharge L3. Under L4: H^s(A)<∞, F001 gives h^s(A)≠∞, so M004 gives dim_H(A)≤s; discharge L4. In particular this holds for zero measure. Under L5: H^s(A)=∞, F001 gives the premise of M005 and hence dim_H(A)≥s; discharge L5. Discharge L1 and universally quantify m,A,s to obtain all the clauses of the asserted conclusion.

H002 makes E bounded, since a compact set in a metric space is bounded. In the Euclidean coordinates this gives F001: there exists L≥1 such that E⊆[-L,L]^n. This includes n=0, where the box denotes the unique point.

Choose L from F001. In the branch L1: n>0, fix a,h0 and assume L2: a>n and L3: 0<h0≤1. Put C=(2L+2)^n. The coordinate grid of mesh h0 covers [-L,L]^n by at most (2L/h0+2)^n≤Ch0^(-n) closed cubes of side at most h0. The Euclidean diameter of each is at most √n h0. Their total a-cost is therefore at most C n^(a/2) h0^(a-n), which tends to zero as h0↓0 because a-n>0. For each positive target scale δ0 choose h0 sufficiently small that √n h0≤δ0. Letting h0 tend to zero then shows H^a_δ0(E)=0 at every positive scale, hence H^a(E)=0. N001 gives D≤a. Since this holds for every a>n, D≤n: if D>n choose a strictly between n and D (or any finite a>n if D=∞). Discharge L1,L2,L3. Record F002: if n>0 then 0≤D≤n; nonnegativity is from N001.

In the branch L4: n=0, H001 implies E=ℝ^0, a singleton. For any b>0 its one-set cover has diameter zero, hence zero b-cost at every scale. Thus H^b(E)=0 for all b>0. N001 gives 0≤D≤b for all b>0, whence D=0. Discharge L4 and combine this with F002 and the exhaustiveness n=0 or n>0. This proves 0≤D≤n<∞ and the singleton assertion when n=0.

Finally fix s,δ and assume L5: s>0 and L6: δ>0. Balls of radius δ/2 centered at points of E are an open cover of E, so H002 provides a finite subcover. Every such ball has diameter at most δ, and the finite sum of their s-costs is finite. The infimum defining H^s_δ(E) is therefore finite. Discharge L5,L6 and quantify s,δ. Together with boundedness in S001 and F003 this is the asserted conclusion.

Fix a>1 (temporary assumption L1). Partition I into N equal closed intervals, N a positive integer. Their diameters are 1/N and their total a-cost is N(1/N)^a=N^(1-a)→0 as N→∞. For every positive target scale these covers are eventually admissible and have costs tending to zero. Thus H^a(I)=0; N001 gives dim_H(I)≤a for every a>1, and hence dim_H(I)≤1. Discharge L1. Record F001: H^a(I)=0 for every a>1 and dim_H(I)≤1.

Fix s,δ, and assume L2: 0<s<1 and L3: δ>0. Consider any countable δ-cover V of I, with nonempty members indexed by K⊆ℕ after discarding empty members; assume this cover condition as L4. Put ρ_i=diam(V_i)≤δ. Fix ε>0 (L5). Each V_i is bounded and nonempty, so inf V_i and sup V_i exist and sup V_i-inf V_i=ρ_i. Define J_i=(inf V_i-ε2^(-i-2),sup V_i+ε2^(-i-2)). Then V_i⊆J_i and |J_i|=ρ_i+ε2^(-i-1). Countable subadditivity of Lebesgue measure, applied to the open intervals covering I, gives 1=|I|≤sum_{i∈K}|J_i|≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i+ε because sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-1)=1. If sum ρ_i=∞ the required inequality is automatic; otherwise let ε↓0 to obtain sum ρ_i≥1. Discharge L5. Record F002: sum_{i∈K}ρ_i≥1.

For each i∈K with ρ_i>0, ρ_i≤δ and s-1<0 imply ρ_i^s=ρ_i·ρ_i^(s-1)≥δ^(s-1)ρ_i. For ρ_i=0 both sides are zero since s>0. Summing nonnegative terms and using F002 gives sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^s≥δ^(s-1)sum_{i∈K}ρ_i≥δ^(s-1). This is true of every δ-cover. Discharge the arbitrary-cover assumption L4 and take the infimum to get F003: H^s_δ(I)≥δ^(s-1).

The bound F003 holds at every δ>0. Since s-1<0, δ^(s-1)→∞ as δ↓0. Thus H^s(I)=∞, and N001 implies dim_H(I)≥s for every 0<s<1. Taking s↑1 gives dim_H(I)≥1; together with F001 this gives dim_H(I)=1 and all the explicit measure clauses of the asserted conclusion. Discharge L2,L3 and universally quantify the indicated exponents and scales.

Fix q,r,ε and temporarily assume L1: n≥1, L2: q>D, L3: 0<r≤1, L4: ε>0. N002 gives D≥0, hence q>0. By N001, H^q(E)=0, so H^q_r(E)=0 by the supremum definition and nonnegativity. The infimum definition, with ε/2>0, gives F001: q>0 and there is a countable cover W of E, with diam(W_i)≤r, whose total q-cost is below ε/2. Pad by empty members to index it by ℕ.

Choose W from F001 and put K={i:W_i≠∅}. Each zero-diameter member is a singleton in a metric space. For i∈K set d_i=min(r,(ε2^(-i-3))^(1/q))>0. When W_i={x}, replace it by the open Euclidean ball of radius d_i/2 centered at its unique point x; otherwise keep W_i. Call the resulting family U and put r_i=diam(U_i). Since n≥1, each replacement has positive diameter d_i≤r and q-cost d_i^q≤ε2^(-i-3)<ε2^(-i-2). Positive-diameter original members still have diameter at most r. Thus U covers E, all its members are nonempty, and all 0<r_i≤r. The added q-cost is at most sum_{i≥0}ε2^(-i-3)=ε/4<ε/2. Therefore sum_{i∈K}r_i^q<ε/2+ε/2=ε. This implements exactly the small singleton enlargements required by the supplied proof.
F002 is the asserted existence conclusion for the arbitrary q,r,ε. Discharge L1,L2,L3,L4 into their stated conditions and quantify q,r,ε, giving the asserted conclusion.

First consider L1: n=0. By N002, E is the singleton ℝ^0 and D=0. The coordinate map t↦((),t) is an isometry from I onto F. 1: # Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
6: Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
7: Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
8: Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).
9: 
10: > 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
11: > \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
12: > \(\mathbb R\).
13: 
14: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
15: 
16: Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
17: 2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
18: \(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
19: the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.
20: 
21: Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
22: compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
23: with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove
24: 
25: \[
26: \dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
27: \]
28: 
29: The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
30: formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
31: 
32: ## Fixed natural-language proof
33: 
34: For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put
35: 
36: \[
37: H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
38:  A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
39: \qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
40: \]
41: 
42: Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
43: unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
44: its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
45: \(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
46: Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
47: measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).
48: 
49: Write \(D=\dim_H E\) and \(F=E\times[0,1]\). First \(0\leq D\leq n\).
50: Indeed, compactness makes \(E\) bounded. When \(n>0\), a box containing
51: it admits a cover by at most \(Ch^{-n}\) cubes of side at most \(h\),
52: for \(0<h\leq1\). Here \(C\) depends only on that box. Each cube has
53: diameter at most \(\sqrt n h\). For any \(s>n\), the total \(s\)-cost
54: is at most \(C n^{s/2}h^{s-n}\to0\). These arbitrarily fine covers
55: give \(H^s(E)=0\) and hence \(D\leq n\). If \(n=0\), nonemptiness
56: makes \(E=\mathbb R^0\), a singleton of zero \(s\)-cost for every
57: \(s>0\); thus \(D=0\).
58: 
59: ### Upper bound
60: 
61: When \(n=0\), \(F\) is isometric to \([0,1]\). Dividing this interval
62: into \(N\) equal pieces gives total \(a\)-cost \(N^{1-a}\to0\) for
63: every \(a>1\), proving \(\dim_H F\leq1=D+1\).

source_steps.text: Fix m≥0 and A⊆ℝ^m, and fix a real s. Temporarily assume L1: s>0. Apply M001 to X=ℝ^m with its Euclidean extended metric and Borel structure, a=s, and set A. For any finite positive scale δ0 its inner infimum is exactly the supplied H^s_δ0(A): nonempty bounded members have the same real and extended diameters, their powers agree, and empty members contribute zero in both conventions. A countable cover can be padded by empty members to be indexed by ℕ; conversely a sequence is countable. The supremum over positive extended scales equals the supremum over positive finite real scales. Indeed both content families increase when the scale decreases, and any fixed finite scale gives at least the content at scale ∞. Thus the term at ∞ cannot increase the supremum. Consequently F001: H^s(A)=h^s(A). No covering-set measurability was used.

The dimension is nonnegative by its supremum definition D004. Still under L1, apply M002, M003, M004 and M005 respectively with X=ℝ^m, its Borel structure, the current set A, and nonnegative exponent s. Under L2: s<dim_H(A), M002 and F001 give H^s(A)=∞; discharge L2. Under L3: dim_H(A)<s, M003 and F001 give H^s(A)=0; discharge L3. Under L4: H^s(A)<∞, F001 gives h^s(A)≠∞, so M004 gives dim_H(A)≤s; discharge L4. In particular this holds for zero measure. Under L5: H^s(A)=∞, F001 gives the premise of M005 and hence dim_H(A)≥s; discharge L5. Discharge L1 and universally quantify m,A,s to obtain all the clauses of the asserted conclusion.

H002 makes E bounded, since a compact set in a metric space is bounded. In the Euclidean coordinates this gives F001: there exists L≥1 such that E⊆[-L,L]^n. This includes n=0, where the box denotes the unique point.

Choose L from F001. In the branch L1: n>0, fix a,h0 and assume L2: a>n and L3: 0<h0≤1. Put C=(2L+2)^n. The coordinate grid of mesh h0 covers [-L,L]^n by at most (2L/h0+2)^n≤Ch0^(-n) closed cubes of side at most h0. The Euclidean diameter of each is at most √n h0. Their total a-cost is therefore at most C n^(a/2) h0^(a-n), which tends to zero as h0↓0 because a-n>0. For each positive target scale δ0 choose h0 sufficiently small that √n h0≤δ0. Letting h0 tend to zero then shows H^a_δ0(E)=0 at every positive scale, hence H^a(E)=0. N001 gives D≤a. Since this holds for every a>n, D≤n: if D>n choose a strictly between n and D (or any finite a>n if D=∞). Discharge L1,L2,L3. Record F002: if n>0 then 0≤D≤n; nonnegativity is from N001.

In the branch L4: n=0, H001 implies E=ℝ^0, a singleton. For any b>0 its one-set cover has diameter zero, hence zero b-cost at every scale. Thus H^b(E)=0 for all b>0. N001 gives 0≤D≤b for all b>0, whence D=0. Discharge L4 and combine this with F002 and the exhaustiveness n=0 or n>0. This proves 0≤D≤n<∞ and the singleton assertion when n=0.

Finally fix s,δ and assume L5: s>0 and L6: δ>0. Balls of radius δ/2 centered at points of E are an open cover of E, so H002 provides a finite subcover. Every such ball has diameter at most δ, and the finite sum of their s-costs is finite. The infimum defining H^s_δ(E) is therefore finite. Discharge L5,L6 and quantify s,δ. Together with boundedness in S001 and F003 this is the asserted conclusion.

Fix a>1 (temporary assumption L1). Partition I into N equal closed intervals, N a positive integer. Their diameters are 1/N and their total a-cost is N(1/N)^a=N^(1-a)→0 as N→∞. For every positive target scale these covers are eventually admissible and have costs tending to zero. Thus H^a(I)=0; N001 gives dim_H(I)≤a for every a>1, and hence dim_H(I)≤1. Discharge L1. Record F001: H^a(I)=0 for every a>1 and dim_H(I)≤1.

Fix s,δ, and assume L2: 0<s<1 and L3: δ>0. Consider any countable δ-cover V of I, with nonempty members indexed by K⊆ℕ after discarding empty members; assume this cover condition as L4. Put ρ_i=diam(V_i)≤δ. Fix ε>0 (L5). Each V_i is bounded and nonempty, so inf V_i and sup V_i exist and sup V_i-inf V_i=ρ_i. Define J_i=(inf V_i-ε2^(-i-2),sup V_i+ε2^(-i-2)). Then V_i⊆J_i and |J_i|=ρ_i+ε2^(-i-1). Countable subadditivity of Lebesgue measure, applied to the open intervals covering I, gives 1=|I|≤sum_{i∈K}|J_i|≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i+ε because sum_{i≥0}2^(-i-1)=1. If sum ρ_i=∞ the required inequality is automatic; otherwise let ε↓0 to obtain sum ρ_i≥1. Discharge L5. Record F002: sum_{i∈K}ρ_i≥1.

For each i∈K with ρ_i>0, ρ_i≤δ and s-1<0 imply ρ_i^s=ρ_i·ρ_i^(s-1)≥δ^(s-1)ρ_i. For ρ_i=0 both sides are zero since s>0. Summing nonnegative terms and using F002 gives sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^s≥δ^(s-1)sum_{i∈K}ρ_i≥δ^(s-1). This is true of every δ-cover. Discharge the arbitrary-cover assumption L4 and take the infimum to get F003: H^s_δ(I)≥δ^(s-1).

The bound F003 holds at every δ>0. Since s-1<0, δ^(s-1)→∞ as δ↓0. Thus H^s(I)=∞, and N001 implies dim_H(I)≥s for every 0<s<1. Taking s↑1 gives dim_H(I)≥1; together with F001 this gives dim_H(I)=1 and all the explicit measure clauses of the asserted conclusion. Discharge L2,L3 and universally quantify the indicated exponents and scales.

Fix q,r,ε and temporarily assume L1: n≥1, L2: q>D, L3: 0<r≤1, L4: ε>0. N002 gives D≥0, hence q>0. By N001, H^q(E)=0, so H^q_r(E)=0 by the supremum definition and nonnegativity. The infimum definition, with ε/2>0, gives F001: q>0 and there is a countable cover W of E, with diam(W_i)≤r, whose total q-cost is below ε/2. Pad by empty members to index it by ℕ.

Choose W from F001 and put K={i:W_i≠∅}. Each zero-diameter member is a singleton in a metric space. For i∈K set d_i=min(r,(ε2^(-i-3))^(1/q))>0. When W_i={x}, replace it by the open Euclidean ball of radius d_i/2 centered at its unique point x; otherwise keep W_i. Call the resulting family U and put r_i=diam(U_i). Since n≥1, each replacement has positive diameter d_i≤r and q-cost d_i^q≤ε2^(-i-3)<ε2^(-i-2). Positive-diameter original members still have diameter at most r. Thus U covers E, all its members are nonempty, and all 0<r_i≤r. The added q-cost is at most sum_{i≥0}ε2^(-i-3)=ε/4<ε/2. Therefore sum_{i∈K}r_i^q<ε/2+ε/2=ε. This implements exactly the small singleton enlargements required by the supplied proof.
F002 is the asserted existence conclusion for the arbitrary q,r,ε. Discharge L1,L2,L3,L4 into their stated conditions and quantify q,r,ε, giving the asserted conclusion.

First consider L1: n=0. By N002, E is the singleton ℝ^0 and D=0. The coordinate map t↦((),t) is an isometry from I onto F. Transporting covers along this map, and in the reverse direction intersecting any ambient cover with its image before taking inverse images, preserves or reduces diameters. Thus all positive-exponent H contents agree for I and F. In particular N003 gives H^a(F)=0 for every a>1; N001 gives dim_H(F)≤a for all a>1 and therefore dim_H(F)≤1=D+1. Discharge L1 and record F001: if n=0 then dim_H(F)≤D+1.

Now assume L2: n≥1. Fix q,δ,ε and temporarily assume L3: q>D, L4: δ>0 and L5: ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ/√2)>0. N002 gives q>0 because D≥0. Apply N004 with these q,r,ε; it gives F002: there exists a countable cover U of E with nonempty members, positive diameters r_i≤r and sum_i r_i^q<ε.

Choose K,U from F002 and set r_i=diam(U_i), N_i=ceil(1/r_i). Partition I into N_i closed intervals of length 1/N_i≤r_i. Since r_i≤1, N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The products of U_i with these intervals cover F, are at most countably many (a countable union of finite families), and have Euclidean diameters at most √2 r_i≤δ. Their total (q+1)-cost is bounded by sum_{i∈K}N_i(√2 r_i)^(q+1)≤2(√2)^(q+1)sum_{i∈K}r_i^q<2(√2)^(q+1)ε. Record F003: there is a countable δ-cover of F of (q+1)-cost below 2(√2)^(q+1)ε.

The infimum defining H^(q+1)_δ(F) is nonnegative and, by F003, is below 2(√2)^(q+1)ε for every ε>0. Let ε↓0 and discharge L5 to obtain H^(q+1)_δ(F)=0. Since the target scale δ>0 was arbitrary, discharge L4 and take the supremum: H^(q+1)(F)=0. N001 implies dim_H(F)≤q+1. N002 says D is finite; since q>D was arbitrary, taking q↓D gives dim_H(F)≤D+1. Explicitly, a strict larger value would admit a q>D with q+1 below that value. Discharge L3 and L2. The natural number n is either 0 or at least 1, so this branch and F001 give the asserted conclusion.

Fix s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and L2: δ>0. Fix an arbitrary countable cover V of F, with nonempty members indexed by K⊆ℕ, under L3: F⊆⋃_{i∈K}V_i and diam(V_i)≤δ for all i. Put ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i=π_{ℝ^n}(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i), and c=H^s_δ(E). The Euclidean product distance shows that both coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz, because each coordinate distance is at most the square root of the sum of the squared coordinate distances. Thus diam(A_i),diam(B_i)≤ρ_i≤δ. Each projected set is nonempty and bounded. By N002, 0≤c<∞. Record these assertions together with the covering property as F001.

Fix ε and assume L4: ε>0. Put η_i=ε2^(-i-1)/(1+ρ_i^s)>0 and J_i=(inf B_i-η_i/2,sup B_i+η_i/2). By F001 the infimum and supremum are finite and sup B_i-inf B_i=diam(B_i)≤ρ_i. Hence B_i⊆J_i and |J_i|≤ρ_i+η_i. Moreover sum_{i∈K}η_iρ_i^s=ε sum_{i∈K}2^(-i-1)ρ_i^s/(1+ρ_i^s)≤ε, using the geometric series on ℕ. Put g_i(t)=ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). These are nonnegative Borel measurable functions: each J_i is open, and each weight is a fixed finite nonnegative number. Record F002: the interval inclusions and length bounds, the error-sum bound, and the measurability of all g_i.

Fix t and temporarily assume L5: t∈I. For an arbitrary x assume L6: x∈E. Then (x,t)∈F, so the cover in F001 supplies i∈K with (x,t)∈V_i. Therefore x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i by F002. Discharge L6 and quantify x: the A_i with t∈J_i cover E and have diameters at most ρ_i≤δ. Their s-cost is at most sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^s1_{J_i}(t)=sum_{i∈K}g_i(t), hence c≤sum_{i∈K}g_i(t) by the definition of H^s_δ(E). Discharge L5 and quantify t. Record F003: for every t∈I, c≤sum_{i∈K}g_i(t).

Integrate F003 with respect to λ|I. Since |I|=1 and c is finite by F001, the integral of the constant c is c. Apply M006 with α=ℝ, μ=λ|I, β=K and functions g_i. The countability and almost-everywhere measurability follow from K⊆ℕ and F002. Each indicator integral is ∫_I g_i=ρ_i^s|J_i∩I|. Thus, in the extended nonnegative reals,
c≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^s|J_i∩I|
 ≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^s(ρ_i+η_i)
 =sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)+sum_{i∈K}η_iρ_i^s
 ≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)+ε.
Here |J_i∩I|≤|J_i|≤ρ_i+η_i by F002. Nonnegative-series addition is valid by taking increasing finite sums, including the cases of infinite sums. Record F004: c≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)+ε.

If sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1)=∞, then c≤that sum immediately. Otherwise F004 and the arbitrariness of ε>0 give c≤sum_{i∈K}ρ_i^(s+1) by letting ε↓0. Discharge L4. The countable δ-cover V was arbitrary, so c is a lower bound for the costs of all such covers, including covers with empty members (which may be discarded without affecting their cost). Discharge L3 and take their infimum: H^s_δ(E)=c≤H^(s+1)_δ(F). Discharge L1,L2 and quantify s,δ to give the asserted conclusion.

Assume L1: D>0, fix s, and assume L2: 0<s<D. N001 gives H^s(E)=∞. By the supremum definition of H this means F001: for every finite M>0 there exists δ>0 with H^s_δ(E)>M. In addition, contents increase as δ decreases, since a smaller scale allows fewer covers. Thus such a bound remains true at every smaller positive scale.
Let M>0 be arbitrary. Choose δ>0 from F001 with H^s_δ(E)>M. Apply N006 at s,δ to obtain H^(s+1)_δ(F)≥H^s_δ(E)>M. Hence H^(s+1)(F)>M. Since M was arbitrary, H^(s+1)(F)=∞. Record this as F002.

N001 and F002 give dim_H(F)≥s+1. Discharge L2 and quantify 0<s<D. N002 says D is finite; under L1 it is positive. Taking the supremum over 0<s<D, or letting s↑D, gives dim_H(F)≥D+1. Discharge L1 to obtain the asserted conditional conclusion.

Assume L1: D=0 and choose x0∈E by H001. Define f:I→F by f(t)=(x0,t). The stipulated Euclidean distance gives dist(f(t),f(u))=|t-u|, so f is an isometric embedding. For every s>0 and δ>0, intersecting any δ-cover of F with f(I) and pulling back by f gives a δ-cover of I with no greater diameters or s-cost. Hence H^s_δ(I)≤H^s_δ(F) and H^s(I)≤H^s(F). This is the required monotonicity and isometry argument, proved directly from covers. For any 0<s<1 (L2), N003 gives H^s(I)=∞ and therefore F001: H^s(F)=∞.

N001 and F001 yield dim_H(F)≥s for every 0<s<1. Discharge L2 and let s↑1 to get dim_H(F)≥1. Under L1, 1=D+1. Discharge L1, proving the asserted conclusion. The construction also applies in n=0 without any change of metric.

N002 says D is a finite nonnegative real, so exactly one of D>0 and D=0 holds. In the first case N007 gives dim_H(F)≥D+1, and in the second N008 gives the same inequality. N005 gives dim_H(F)≤D+1 in both cases. Antisymmetry therefore yields dim_H(F)=D+1=dim_H(E)+1. By the definitions F=E×I and I=[0,1], this is the requested equality dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1. All distances used are the prescribed Euclidean distances, and the preceding case statements include n=0.

70: The positive-diameter requirement costs nothing: start with a cover of
71: cost below \(\varepsilon/2\); replace each zero-diameter singleton by
72: a ball of diameter at most \(r\), choosing the \(i\)-th replacement
73: to have \(q\)-cost less than \(\varepsilon2^{-i-2}\). The added cost
74: is less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Discard empty members.
75: 
76: Let \(N_i=\lceil1/r_i\rceil\). Partition \([0,1]\) into \(N_i\)
77: closed intervals of length \(1/N_i\leq r_i\). Because \(r_i\leq1\),
78: \(N_i\leq2/r_i\). The corresponding products with \(U_i\) form a
79: countable cover of \(F\). Each has Euclidean diameter at most
80: \(\sqrt2 r_i\), and their total \((q+1)\)-cost is at most
81: 
82: \[
83: \sum_iN_i(\sqrt2 r_i)^{q+1}
84: \leq2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\sum_i r_i^q
85: <2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\varepsilon.
86: \]
87: 
88: For any target scale \(\delta>0\), choose
89: \(r\leq\min(1,\delta/\sqrt2)\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
90: Thus \(H^{q+1}_\delta(F)=0\) for every scale, so
91: \(H^{q+1}(F)=0\) and \(\dim_H F\leq q+1\). Letting \(q\downarrow D\)
92: gives \(\dim_H F\leq D+1\).
93: 
94: ### Lower bound when \(D>0\)
95: 
96: Fix \(0<s<D\). Then \(H^s(E)=\infty\), so
97: \(H^s_\delta(E)\) becomes arbitrarily large as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
98: We claim that, for every \(\delta>0\),
99: 
100: \[
101: H^s_\delta(E)\leq H^{s+1}_\delta(F).                 \tag{1}
102: \]
103: 
104: Take an arbitrary countable \(\delta\)-cover \((V_i)_{i\geq0}\) of
105: \(F\), discarding empty members. Define
106: \(\rho_i=\operatorname{diam}V_i\),
107: \(A_i=\pi_{\mathbb R^n}(V_i)\), and
108: \(B_i=\pi_{\mathbb R}(V_i)\). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz,
109: so both projected diameters are at most \(\rho_i\leq\delta\).
110: For \(\varepsilon>0\), put
111: 
112: \[
113: \eta_i=\frac{\varepsilon2^{-i-1}}{1+\rho_i^s}>0.
114: \]
115: 
116: Enclose \(B_i\) in an open interval \(J_i\) of length at most
117: \(\rho_i+\eta_i\): its supremum minus infimum is at most \(\rho_i\),
118: and an enlargement of total width \(\eta_i\) suffices. This avoids
119: assuming that the arbitrary covering sets or their projections are measurable.
120: 
121: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), the sets \(A_i\) for which \(t\in J_i\)
122: cover \(E\). Indeed, a point \((x,t)\in F\) belongs to some \(V_i\),
123: giving \(x\in A_i\) and \(t\in B_i\subset J_i\). Their diameters
124: are at most \(\rho_i\). Consequently, with \(c=H^s_\delta(E)\),
125: 
126: \[
127: c\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s\mathbf1_{J_i}(t)\quad(t\in[0,1]).
128: \]
129: 
130: The constant \(c\) is finite: compactness gives a finite cover of \(E\)
131: by balls of diameter at most \(\delta\), with finite \(s\)-cost.
132: Each summand is nonnegative and measurable since \(J_i\) is open.
133: Integrate over \([0,1]\), of Lebesgue measure one, and use Tonelli's
134: theorem for this nonnegative series. Since
135: \(|J_i\cap[0,1]|\leq\rho_i+\eta_i\),
136: 
137: \[
138: \begin{aligned}
139: c&\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s|J_i\cap[0,1]|\\
140:  &\leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\sum_i\eta_i\rho_i^s
141:  \leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\varepsilon.
142: \end{aligned}
143: \]
144: 
145: If the first series is infinite the desired inequality is immediate;
146: otherwise let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Take the infimum over the
147: arbitrary covers to obtain (1). As its left side is unbounded at small
148: scales, \(H^{s+1}(F)=\infty\), giving \(\dim_H F\geq s+1\).
149: Letting \(s\uparrow D\) proves \(\dim_H F\geq D+1\).
150: 
151: ### Lower bound when \(D=0\)
152: 
153: Choose \(x_0\in E\). The map \(t\mapsto(x_0,t)\) is an isometric
154: embedding of \([0,1]\) into \(F\), so dimension monotonicity gives
155: \(\dim_H F\geq\dim_H[0,1]\). This interval has dimension one:
156: equal-length covers gave the upper bound above. For \(0<s<1\), any
157: \(\delta\)-cover with diameters \(\rho_i\leq\delta\) satisfies
158: \(\sum_i\rho_i\geq1\). To see this, enclose its nonempty members
159: in open intervals of lengths at most \(\rho_i+\varepsilon2^{-i-1}\),
160: use countable subadditivity of length to get
161: \(1\leq\sum_i\rho_i+\varepsilon\), and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
162: Hence \(\sum_i\rho_i^s\geq\delta^{s-1}\sum_i\rho_i
163: \geq\delta^{s-1}\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
164: This proves the lower bound one. Thus \(\dim_H F\geq1=D+1\),
165: including when \(n=0\).
166: 
167: Together the bounds establish the required equality.

abbrev GDVec (m : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)

def GDInterval : Set ℝ := Set.Icc 0 1

def GDPoint {m : ℕ} (x : GDVec m) (t : ℝ) : GDVec (m + 1) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.snoc (fun i => x i) t)

def GDProduct {m : ℕ} (A : Set (GDVec m)) : Set (GDVec (m + 1)) :=
  {z | ∃ x ∈ A, ∃ t ∈ GDInterval, z = GDPoint x t}

def GDCost {X : Type*} [PseudoEMetricSpace X] (s : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (_ : A.Nonempty), (Metric.ediam A) ^ s

  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i)

    ∑' i, GDCost s (U i)
